lessonTitle: Combustion: Air-Fuel Ratio, Enthalpy of Formation and Flame Temperature

blocks.text: A natural-gas boiler in a hospital burns methane with just enough air. If the air supply drifts 20% high, flame temperature drops and the stack loses more heat; if it drifts low, carbon monoxide and soot appear. To tune it, the engineer needs the air-fuel ratio, the heat released per kilogram of fuel, and an estimate of the flame temperature. All three follow from atom balances and enthalpies of formation.

blocks.markdown: **Combustion** is rapid oxidation of a fuel. For a hydrocarbon $C_xH_y$ the complete products are $CO_2$ and $H_2O$. Air is modelled as 21% $O_2$ and 79% $N_2$ by mole, so each kmol of $O_2$ comes with 3.76 kmol of $N_2$ (nitrogen is inert here and appears unchanged in the products). **Stoichiometric** (theoretical) air is exactly the amount needed for complete combustion; **excess air** is any amount beyond that, usually expressed as a percentage.

blocks.caption: Stoichiometric reaction on a molar basis. Balance C, then H, then O, and N last.
With excess air of $e$ (fraction), multiply the stoichiometric air by $(1+e)$; the extra $O_2$ and its $N_2$ pass unburnt to the products.

blocks.title: Balancing methane and finding AF
blocks.prompt: Burn methane ($CH_4$, $M = 16.04$ kg/kmol) completely with the theoretical amount of air. Write the balanced equation and find the air-fuel ratio on mole and mass bases.

steps.text: Carbon: 1 C gives 1 $CO_2$; hydrogen: 4 H gives 2 $H_2O$; oxygen needed: $1 + 1 = 2$ kmol $O_2$, so $a_{th} = 2$. Nitrogen: $3.76 \times 2 = 7.52$.
Moles of air per kmol of fuel.

blocks.answer: Mole basis: 9.52 kmol air/kmol fuel. Mass basis: AF = 17.19 kg air per kg fuel.

blocks.markdown: **First law for a reacting system.** For steady flow with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes and no shaft work, $Q = \sum N_p\,\bar h_p - \sum N_r\,\bar h_r$, where each absolute enthalpy is the **enthalpy of formation** $\bar h_f^\circ$ (at 25 °C, 1 atm) plus the sensible enthalpy $\Delta\bar h = \bar h(T) - \bar h(298\ \mathrm{K})$. Elements in their stable state at 25 °C and 1 atm (such as $O_2$ and $N_2$) have $\bar h_f^\circ = 0$.

blocks.latex: Q = \sum_p N_p\left(\bar h_f^\circ + \Delta\bar h\right)_p - \sum_r N_r\left(\bar h_f^\circ + \Delta\bar h\right)_r
blocks.caption: Units kJ per kmol of fuel; $Q < 0$ means heat is released to the surroundings.

blocks.title: Heat released and adiabatic flame temperature of methane
blocks.prompt: Methane and theoretical air enter at 25 °C. (a) Find the heat released per kmol and per kg if the products leave at 25 °C with water as vapour. (b) Estimate the adiabatic flame temperature using the typical sensible enthalpies in the table below.

steps.text: Reactants and products at 25 °C use formation enthalpies only. Reactants: $\bar h_f$ = -74 850 (O2 and N2 are zero). Products: $1(-393\,520) + 2(-241\,820)$.
Adiabatic: $Q = 0$, so the products' sensible enthalpy equals the heat released, $\sum N_p\Delta\bar h_p = 802\,310$ kJ/kmol. Try 2200 K using the table (CO2 103 560, H2O 83 150, N2 63 360).
That is below 802 310, so T is higher. Try 2400 K (CO2 115 780, H2O 93 740, N2 70 640).
Linear interpolation between the two trials.

blocks.answer: Q = -802 310 kJ/kmol (50 020 kJ/kg, heat released); T_ad is about 2327 K.

blocks.caption: Typical sensible enthalpies $\Delta\bar h = \bar h(T) - \bar h(298\ \mathrm{K})$ in kJ/kmol (approximate, rounded).

blocks.markdown: The adiabatic flame temperature is **iterated**: guess $T$, evaluate $\sum N_p\Delta\bar h_p$, compare with the heat released, and interpolate to the temperature at which they are equal. The result is an estimate. Real flames are cooler because of dissociation of $CO_2$ and $H_2O$, heat loss, incomplete combustion and variable specific heats. Excess air dilutes the products, so more moles must be heated by the same heat release and the flame temperature falls.

blocks.title: Higher and lower heating value
blocks.text: The **higher heating value** (HHV) assumes water leaves as liquid; the **lower heating value** (LHV) assumes water vapour. For methane the HHV is about 890 330 kJ/kmol (55507 kJ/kg) and the LHV about 802 310 kJ/kmol (50019 kJ/kg).

items: Balance carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and finally nitrogen.
$AF$ on a mass basis uses molar masses; $M_{air} = 28.97$ kg/kmol.
Excess air $e$: air supplied $= (1+e)\times$ stoichiometric; extra $O_2$ appears in the products.
Use enthalpy of formation at 25 °C plus sensible enthalpy at the actual temperature.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Do not give $N_2$ or $O_2$ a nonzero formation enthalpy. Do not forget the $N_2$ in the products when computing flame temperature (it carries most of the heat capacity). State whether water is vapour or liquid when quoting a heating value.

points: $AF = N_{air} M_{air}/(N_{fuel} M_{fuel})$ and excess air multiplies the theoretical air.
Steady-flow heat release: $Q = \sum N_p(\bar h_f + \Delta\bar h)_p - \sum N_r(\bar h_f + \Delta\bar h)_r$.
Adiabatic flame temperature is found by iterating $\sum N_p\Delta\bar h_p$ until it equals the heat released.

questions.stem: For complete stoichiometric combustion of propane, $C_3H_8 + a(O_2 + 3.76N_2) \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O + \dots$, how many kmol of $O_2$ are needed per kmol of propane?

distractorRationale.a: Counts only the oxygen needed for hydrogen or an incorrect carbon balance.

questions.explanation: Oxygen atoms in the products are $3\times2 + 4\times1 = 10$, so $a = 5$ kmol of $O_2$. It also follows from $a = x + y/4 = 3 + 2 = 5$.

questions.stem: A steady-flow combustor with no work output loses heat to the surroundings. In the energy equation $Q = H_{products} - H_{reactants}$, what is the sign of $Q$ and what does it mean?

options.text: $Q$ is negative: heat leaves the combustor
$Q$ is positive: heat leaves the combustor
$Q$ is positive: heat enters the combustor

questions.correctOptionText: $Q$ is negative: heat leaves the combustor

distractorRationale.b: Positive $Q$ means heat enters the system in this convention.

questions.explanation: The convention is heat added to the system as positive. Since the product enthalpy at the same temperature is lower than the reactant enthalpy, $Q < 0$ and heat is released.

questions.stem: Excess air is added to a combustor while the fuel flow and inlet temperatures are unchanged. What happens to the adiabatic flame temperature?

options.text: It increases, because more oxygen gives more heat
It is unchanged, since the fuel energy is unchanged
It increases because the nitrogen reacts
It decreases, because the same heat release warms a larger mass of products

questions.correctOptionText: It decreases, because the same heat release warms a larger mass of products

distractorRationale.a: The heat released is set by the fuel; extra oxygen does not add heat.
distractorRationale.b: The same energy is spread across more moles, so the temperature falls.

questions.explanation: The heat release is fixed by the amount of fuel burned. The extra $O_2$ and $N_2$ pass through as additional product moles, so the temperature rise for the same energy is smaller.

questions.stem: Isooctane ($C_8H_{18}$, $M = 114.23$ kg/kmol) is burnt with theoretical air ($M_{air} = 28.97$ kg/kmol). What is the air-fuel ratio on a mass basis?

distractorRationale.a: This is the mole ratio of air to fuel (12.5 × 4.76), not a mass ratio.
distractorRationale.c: Uses the oxygen moles as a mass ratio.
distractorRationale.d: Ignores the nitrogen in the air.

questions.explanation: Stoichiometric oxygen is $a = 8 + 18/4 = 12.5$ kmol, so air is $12.5\times4.76 = 59.5$ kmol per kmol fuel. Mass AF $= 59.5\times28.97/114.23 = 15.09$.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has a standard enthalpy of formation of zero at 25 °C and 1 atm?

distractorRationale.a: Formed from elements with a nonzero heat of formation (-110 530 kJ/kmol).

questions.explanation: By convention the enthalpy of formation of every element in its stable form at the reference state is zero. $O_2$ is the stable form of oxygen, while the compounds have formation enthalpies that depend on their stability.

questions.stem: Propane ($C_3H_8$, $M = 44.10$ kg/kmol) is burnt with 20% excess air ($M_{air} = 28.97$ kg/kmol). Find the air-fuel ratio in kg of air per kg of fuel.
questions.explanation: Theoretical air is $5\times4.76 = 23.8$ kmol per kmol of fuel, and 20% excess gives $23.8\times1.2 = 28.56$ kmol. Then $AF = 28.56\times28.97/44.10 = 18.76$.

questions.stem: A burner consumes 0.015 kg/s of butane ($C_4H_{10}$ gas, $M = 58.12$ kg/kmol) with reactants and products at 25 °C and the water leaving as vapour. Use $\bar h_f$ of -126 150 ($C_4H_{10}$), -393 520 ($CO_2$) and -241 820 ($H_2O$ vapour) kJ/kmol. Find the heat release rate in kW.
questions.explanation: Per kmol: heat released $= -[4(-393\,520) + 5(-241\,820) - (-126\,150)] = 2\,657\,030$ kJ/kmol, or 45716 kJ/kg. Multiplying by 0.015 kg/s gives 685.7 kW.

questions.stem: Ethane ($C_2H_6$ gas, $\bar h_f = -84\,680$ kJ/kmol) burns completely with 20% excess air, entering at 25 °C, and the combustor is adiabatic. The products are 2 $CO_2$, 3 $H_2O$ (vapour), 0.7 $O_2$ and 15.792 $N_2$ per kmol of fuel. Use $\bar h_f$ of -393 520 ($CO_2$) and -241 820 ($H_2O$) kJ/kmol and the typical sensible enthalpies (kJ/kmol): at 2000 K CO2 91 440, H2O 72 790, N2 56 140, O2 59 180; at 2200 K CO2 103 560, H2O 83 150, N2 63 360, O2 66 800. Estimate the adiabatic flame temperature in K by linear interpolation between 2000 K and 2200 K.
Define the higher and lower heating values of a fuel. Using enthalpies of formation, show that for methane the HHV exceeds the LHV and explain which is appropriate for a condensing boiler.
markingGuide: HHV: heat released when products are cooled to the reference temperature with water condensed to liquid; LHV: water remains vapour
Uses $Q = \sum N_r\bar h_f - \sum N_p\bar h_f$ for products at 25 °C
The difference is the latent heat of the water formed: $2\times(285\,830-241\,820) = 88\,020$ kJ/kmol
A condensing boiler recovers latent heat, so its efficiency should be quoted against the HHV, while a non-condensing boiler is usually quoted against the LHV
questions.explanation: Methane's HHV is 55507 kJ/kg and its LHV is 50019 kJ/kg. The difference is the latent heat of the 2 kmol of water formed, which a condensing boiler can recover.

questions.stem: Describe how the adiabatic flame temperature of a fuel burnt in air is estimated by iteration. Explain why the estimate exceeds the temperature measured in real flames, and what effect increasing excess air has.
markingGuide: Reactants at 25 °C: heat release equals $\sum N_r\bar h_f - \sum N_p\bar h_f$
Guess $T_p$ and compute $\sum N_p\Delta\bar h_p$ from tables including $N_2$ and any excess $O_2$
Compare with the heat release; adjust $T$ and interpolate until they match
Real flames are cooler: dissociation of $CO_2$ and $H_2O$, incomplete combustion, heat loss, radiation and variable specific heats
More excess air increases the number of product moles, so the temperature falls
Notes that the result is an estimate and depends on tabulated data quality
questions.explanation: The flame temperature is found by guessing $T$, evaluating the products' sensible enthalpy and interpolating until it equals the heat released. Dissociation and heat losses lower real flames, and excess air dilutes the products, lowering the temperature further.
